name: Yamnaya culture
title: The story of the Yamnaya culture

text: More than 5,000 years ago, the Yamnaya lived on the steppe of today’s Ukraine and southern Russia.
Their name comes from a Russian word about pits, after their pit graves.
src: c. 3300–2600 BCE / The Pontic–Caspian steppe between the Southern Bug, Dniester and Ural rivers, in present-day Ukraine and southern Russia
‘Yamnaya’ is an archaeologists’ label from a Russian word meaning ‘related to pits’, after the pit graves under burial mounds

text: They were herders who moved their animals across the steppe.
They travelled in carts and wagons, probably pulled by oxen, and perhaps rode horses too.
src: Its people moved their herds across the steppe in carts and wagons
two-wheeled carts and four-wheeled wagons, thought to have been drawn by oxen at this time / whether they also rode horses is disputed

text: Chiefs led their groups, and metalworkers were held in special honour.
They probably ate meat, milk, yogurt and cheese.
src: Society was organised in chiefdoms. Metalworkers and other craftsmen held a special status
Anthony speculates that they ate meat, milk, yogurt, cheese and soups of seeds and wild vegetables

text: Some of the dead were laid under earth mounds called kurgans, covered in ochre, a coloured earth.
Some important people were buried with whole wooden wagons.
src: The dead were laid on their backs with their knees bent and covered in ochre, in simple pits under kurgans / Kurgan burial may have been rare, perhaps reserved for special adults
In some areas elite members of the Yamnaya culture were buried with complete wooden wagons

text: Many scholars think they spoke an early form of the Indo-European languages.
DNA links them to many later people of Europe and South Asia, though scholars debate how far.
src: The widely accepted Kurgan hypothesis holds that they spoke a stage of Proto-Indo-European / Its importance today lies above all in the question of the Indo-European languages
DNA links them to much later European and South Asian ancestry, though critics question how far
